https://www.dw.com/en/russia-s-hybrid-at.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KZNu Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes like this one also take off from Leipzig, carrying military supplies for Ukraine Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4 , a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine . The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible . But now the government has announced its findings. On Tuesday, September 1, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort." Back in late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter. However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet." Exactly how and when remains unclear, however. Mixed reactions to measures For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag , however, this does not go far enough. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in an interview with DW. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said. Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement." However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter demands, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia flatly denies responsibility for the Leipzig incident? President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures. Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target." A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats. Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war." In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said. Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, Green Party lawmaker Sara Nanni fears that Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she told DW, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act." Not at war with Russia From a strictly legal standpoint, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4. But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts argue that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage. However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Sönke Marahrens believes that Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens says. He went on to say that, "If Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions (to support Ukraine), that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines." The AfD factor and the Saxony-Anhalt election The state elections coming up on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt are one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far-right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state. The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen as none of Germany's business and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine. What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This is why the federal government — composed of the conservate CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner. This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia. This article was translated from German. https://english.news.cn/europe/20260826/.text: EU should pursue "friendly competition" with China, not trade barriers: Slovak PM BRATISLAVA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly competition" with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Their discussions covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." On the EU's next long-term budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. The two leaders also discussed EU enlargement. Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, but said all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily

https://nineoclock.ro/romanian-foreign-m.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu meets UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London Nine O’Clock received the following information from Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MAE) regarding the meeting. Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu held a bilateral meeting in London on Thursday, September 3, 2026, with the UK Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, Ed Miliband. The meeting had four priorities on the agenda: the Romanian diaspora in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, economic cooperation, security, and cooperation in the fields of education and culture. Strong bilateral partnership The Romanian official highlighted the strong bilateral framework established by the Strategic Partnership, updated through the Joint Declaration signed in London in 2023, as well as the results of the resumption of the bilateral strategic dialogue in October last year. Trade exceeds €10 billion On the economic front, the two officials assessed the current state of bilateral economic relations, with trade exceeding €10 billion, as well as key areas for growth. The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland ranks 11th among foreign direct investors in Romania, with more than 7,000 companies with British capital registered in the country and jobs supported jointly, including through access to the Single Market. At the same time, Romanian entrepreneurs are showing growing interest in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Minister Oana Țoiu highlighted sectors with significant growth potential, such as advanced technologies, financial services and the agri-food sector. In the latter case, Romanian exports to the British market recorded significant growth last year. Security cooperation and the Black Sea Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu thanked the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland for the solidarity it has shown towards Romania, particularly for the enhanced air policing mission conducted by the Royal Air Force on Romanian territory between March and July 2026. The two officials discussed the security of trade in the Black Sea and the role of the Port of Constanța, as well as the role of British expertise in this area and in protecting critical maritime infrastructure. More than one million Romanians in the UK Minister Oana Țoiu also highlighted the outstanding contribution of the more than one million Romanian citizens living in the United Kingdom to strengthening bilateral relations. The agenda included discussions on British schools hosting courses in Romanian Language, Culture and Civilisation, as well as the activity of Romanian language lectorates at the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge. The officials also discussed the activity of the British Council in Romania, the United Kingdom joining the Erasmus+ programme, discussions on mobility schemes for young people and teachers, as well as facilitating the mutual recognition of diplomas and qualifications. Romania’s OECD accession The two ministers also discussed Romania’s accession to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a process in which Romania has completed all the technical criteria for accession over the past year. Romania is relying on its partnership with the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in this process, particularly given the positive impact that OECD membership is expected to have on investment. EU-UK cooperation on foreign policy and security The two ministers also discussed preparations for the future European Union–United Kingdom Summit, with a view to deepening cooperation in the fields of foreign policy, security and defence. Romania’s diplomatic history showcased in London The history of diplomatic cooperation between Romania and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland will also be part of the London Festival of Architecture. From September 18 to 20, Romania will open to visitors the building that previously housed the Romanian Embassy in London and which currently serves as the headquarters of the Romanian Cultural Institute (ICR). Ed Miliband was appointed Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs on 20 July 2026. He was previously Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero between 5 July 2024 and 20 July 2026. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Ihor Malchevsky, a deputy department head at Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv, escapes from the building after it was hit by a Russian drone strike on Monday. Photograph: Thomas Peter/Reuters View image in fullscreen Ihor Malchevsky, a deputy department head at Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv, escapes from the building after it was hit by a Russian drone strike on Monday. Photograph: Thomas Peter/Reuters Opinion Ukraine I went curtain shopping during a Kyiv air raid. And not because I’m ‘resilient’ Diana Berg We can’t count on tomorrow so it would be rational to own less. Yet we make our homes nicer, just to anchor ourselves in the here and now Fri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.59 EDT Share I was standing in front of a locked basement door in a building in our neighbourhood, laughing, as Ukrainian air defence shot down drones directly above me. I had run into the first residential building I could reach, and I even took a photo of the locked door – a shelter, and the shelter locked – because I wanted to remember it. I was on my way to buy curtains. I hadn’t checked whether there was an alert before I left home. I had simply set out for the shop, 20 minutes away through our residential district, on foot. But somewhere along the way, things started exploding in the sky above me – and I was suddenly walking through a city under attack because I had decided that my windows needed new curtains. What the fuck was I laughing at? I should have been terrified, and I was. It was just that I still wanted the curtains, and the absurdity was hilarious. The curtain shop was closed because of the raid – this international chain, it turns out, shuts when the sirens go off , unlike many Ukrainian-owned stores. So I came back the next day and bought them. They are better than the old ones and cover the windows properly. Only after I had hung them did I realise that they also let me see less of the war from my sofa: the flashes of air defence , the smoke, whatever was happening outside. I had not made the war any safer. I had only made it slightly harder to see. I had been away from Kyiv for a month and while I was gone, the rhythm of the war, which I have lived with for years, had changed: attacks now came by day , alerts could swallow half of it, and explosions, drones and smoke had become part of the daytime soundscape in a way that felt new even to me. My response, apparently, was to buy curtains. In January 2022, back in Mariupol, when everyone around us was waiting for Russia to invade, my husband bought an expensive coffee machine. I thought it was ridiculous. He told me he was tired of living in fear and anticipation, that he wanted to live here and now, and that if the machine survived only a couple of weeks he didn’t care. Since the full-scale invasion, he has bought a television, an electronic piano, a huge monitor for my laptop, a washing machine and a dryer – every year something large that could be smashed in a second. View image in fullscreen Diana Berg outside a locked shelter door during an air raid in Kyiv. Photograph: Diana Berg We don’t do the big things. Our flooring still needs repairing, and the flat we have lived in since we fled Mariupol in 2022 needs renovation. We don’t invest in it because spending serious money, time and energy on a place a missile could destroy tomorrow feels slightly insane. There is a strange logic in this, a logic that isn’t really there when I look at it closely. But the small things keep sneaking in. I left all my books in Mariupol. When we fled, they were not exactly high on the evacuation priority list, and later they were lost when our rented flat was destroyed in the airstrike on the Drama Theatre . I started buying books again in Kyiv, one at a time, and somehow I now have a bookcase full of them. We got plants. We got cats – four now, two from Mariupol and two adopted during the full-scale war. One of them can barely see, barely hear and limps after an accident; we chose him in 2023, apparently deciding that what our lives really needed was another vulnerable creature to worry about. The rational wartime strategy would be to own less, need less, attach yourself to less. We have left home twice, both times with only what we could carry, so nobody needs to explain to us what attachment costs. It isn’t that we don’t know what can happen. Last week a building belonging to my husband’s workplace was hit. He was in a different one, but he could have been there, and I don’t know how to convey that fear. I keep my Instagram mostly to cats, standup, sport, beauty and interiors, because I don’t want to spend every waking hour looking at war – but the news gets through even those filters. In my feed I saw a post from a soldier at the front, showing footage from the site of that building: the car park, the burnt-out cars, and the news that his wife, who had worked with my husband, had been killed there. There were photographs of the two of them walking into the new house they had bought and planned to renovate, the walls still bare, the new car they had bought 10 days earlier – and then that same car, gutted in the car park along with everything around it. She had been inside. It was one and the same strike. What is there to say? During an attack, we have our own little scale of urgency. Ballistic missile: bathroom. Now. Cruise missile: you can finish your coffee. Drones take the longest, so you can usually carry on. For now. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion In fact, I am writing this column from the bathroom, the safest place in the flat. There is an air-raid alert and I can hear air defence outside; the four cats are with me. On Telegram, people post live videos from all over Kyiv, often before anything appears in the official news, and as I write this, Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv is on fire . One person has been killed. People are climbing out of upper-floor windows on to fire ladders. I am sitting in the bathtub, watching it live on my phone and writing about curtains. During another alert that lasted through the afternoon and into the night, we visited friends for a Sunday barbecue. We sat outside while something was burning or being intercepted somewhere above us; meanwhile, someone turned meat on the grill and my friend’s mum told me about the new flowers in her garden. At some point I had the very clear thought that, theoretically, something could fall straight on to my plate. Then I looked back at the flowers. This is what I find difficult about the word “resilience”, so often used about people living in war zones. It sounds like a virtue, something noble you develop when tested – but it feels much less noble than that. The curtains hide a little of the war from me. I feel guilty for shutting my eyes to the horror outside, but in reality it’s more like refusing to allow the war to make every decision. So the curtains are hanging now. They make the room warmer and they cover the windows better. The photo of the locked door is still on my phone. Next: I need to paint the walls in the bathroom. I’ve already chosen the colour. Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government kills motorway deal, files criminal complaint against Fidesz-era oligarchs The government will terminate the contract concluded on the motorway concession, will file a criminal complaint, and criminal proceedings will be launched, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced at a government press conference in Budapest. Péter Magyar stated that, based on the facts and the ministry’s detailed professional examination, the government had reached a completely unambiguous and irreversible decision. “This contract, in this form, is over” — the government will no longer maintain a situation in which, from the work of Hungarian people, “we enrich the circle of the failed Fidesz party elite and oligarchs for decades,” he said. He said the government’s task is clear and unambiguous: they will protect taxpayers’ money and will use every lawful and legal means to terminate the contract. They will not allow “Hungary to be extorted for decades to come,” while at the same time they cannot allow the safe operation of the motorways to be put at risk for even a single second, he explained. In his view, the case involves an at least 23,000 billion forint, partially realised “attempt to seize public funds,” suspicion of serious violations of EU and national law, and massive overpricing. In Hungary, the era of governing without consequences is over — “not a single contract is untouchable if it was born to plunder the nation,” the Prime Minister declared. He noted that he would not be surprised if the case were also to attract the interest of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office. The prime minister also spoke about the fact that, under Hungarian criminal procedure rules, compensation for damages caused is considered a mitigating circumstance in criminal proceedings. He sent a message to those involved, urging them not to obstruct the swift takeover of the motorway network’s operation and to cooperate fully with the state in all respects. Péter Magyar also said that the MNB scandal is “small change” compared to the motorway concession, that certain decisions concerning Magyar Koncessziós Infrastruktúra Fejlesztő (MKIF) Zrt. had been made beyond a single government cycle, and that they had attempted to determine Hungary’s room for manoeuvre — and the situation of the Hungarian budget and Hungarian public funds — for decades to come. The 35-year motorway concession is Europe’s largest such concession agreement and involves more than 23,000 billion forints, he added. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said that if this contract were to remain in force, “Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj would be enriched by 3,633 billion forints from Hungarian taxpayers’ funds by 2057.” If the contract were left in force, the state would have to pay a net 363 billion forints in 2027 — equivalent to a net 41.4 million forints per hour going to Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj for operating the motorways, he pointed out. He stated that this contract is unsustainable and unlawful, while also stressing that it is important to recognise that “this contract has essentially plundered Magyar Közút.” MKIF Zrt. took over all motorway engineering directorates from Magyar Közút — meaning they also took over the state’s capacity to operate the motorways, he said. He emphasised that if this contract were terminated overnight, the state would be unable to operate the motorways, as the engineering depots cannot be replaced at short notice. The concessionaire’s cooperation is in any case necessary in order to terminate the contract and for Magyar Közút to retake control of operations, he believed. Dávid Vitézy stated that approximately two-thirds of Hungary’s motorways had been handed over for operation to MKIF, the motorway concession company associated with the names of Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj. The contract runs for nine parliamentary terms, i.e. until 2057. It was signed in 2022, following the elections, by Antal Rogán, the minister heading the Cabinet Office of the Prime Minister, he explained. He noted that the European Commission is currently also conducting infringement proceedings against Hungary in connection with the procedure. The minister stated that the government considers the motorway concession contract unlawful because, in its view, it does not constitute a genuine concession, as the state has assumed all risks from MKIF. “This is not a genuine concession,” the minister declared. He justified this by explaining that a concession contract is built on — and can last 35 years for — the purpose of placing some form of risk on the concessionaire: the price at which it can invest and build, how it can organise operations, and how these costs are recouped over the long duration. Dávid Vitézy argued, however, that MKIF had “not for a single moment” borne any such risk — that it might end up solving something at a higher cost than planned, or that unforeseen circumstances might arise during construction — because the Hungarian state had assumed every risk. Dávid Vitézy stated that it was therefore questionable whether this was in fact a concession contract at all, because if it was not, then it had been unlawful from the outset, was unlawful in every respect, and could not be maintained lawfully. The government would like to terminate the concession contract from the end of the year, but doing so also requires the cooperation of the concessionaire. He noted that disputes are to be settled not by a Hungarian court but by an international arbitration tribunal. He added that if MKIF is uncooperative, protracted arbitration proceedings lasting several years could follow. He said that while “the fallen prime minister” constantly envisions foreigners behind every topic, it was the previous government that handed Budapest Airport over to French operators, issued a concession tender for the airport railway on which only foreign companies competed, entrusted the Budapest–Belgrade railway line to the Chinese, and gave Paks II and the metro renovation to the Russians. He announced that the total cost of planned motorway developments in Hungary amounts to more than ten thousand billion forints. The Ministry of Transport will carry out a reassessment, prioritisation, and technical, social and economic review of these projects, on the basis of which the government will be able to make decisions on their implementation, he explained. At the same time, he stressed that in recent years practically zero forints had gone toward the maintenance of single- and double-digit national main roads. It is therefore necessary to weigh what investments can be carried out in light of the budget’s capacity to bear the burden, he said. https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-viral-v.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OAn7 Riyadh's King Khalid International Aiport has been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis Image: Social Media/REUTERS Advertisement Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in recent days. At least 16 people have been killed since last Thursday, according to Saudi authorities. As news of the attacks spreads, social media users have been sharing videos that they claim show the strikes. While some authentic footage of the attacks and their aftermath has circulated online, DW Fact check found that several viral videos are not genuine and show signs of being AI-generated. This AI-generated video has been circulating since March and contains several inconsistencies Image: X Claim : This post with 1.7 million views on X, claims it shows the moment of an attack on the airport. DW Fact check : Fake The video has been online since March 2026 and could not show the most recent attacks on the airport. Hectic camera movements and blurry footage help conceal glitches that often point to AI-generated content. However, our frame-by-frame analysis identified several inconsistencies. That suggests the video was AI-generated. In the video, people run toward an exit as an explosion occurs outside. Despite the apparent danger, they continue moving toward the blast, seemingly through a glass door. This reaction is implausible. Around 10 seconds into the video, an image of a hand holding a smartphone appears on the side of a man's head. At 12 seconds, one man first appears not to have a hand, then miraculously has one. A side-by-side comparison shows a hand appear out of nowhere Image: X Meta's AI identification tool finds AI signatures in the video and concludes it was created using generative AI. Many shared the video as authentic, including the Times of Israel – its post had more than 256,000 views at the time of writing. The video has appeared in many languages, including Arabic , English , Russian , Spanish , Turkish , Nepali , and it has been shared on YouTube , Instagram , TikTok , Facebook and other platforms. AI generates video from real photograph Claim : In this post on X with 2.9 million views, a user claims it shows "new video footage of the moment King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted." AI can generate videos from still photographs Image: X DW Fact check : Fake The video is AI-generated and contains several inconsistencies when compared with the real airport. Using a reverse image search, we found the photograph used to generate the fake video. The original image was uploaded to stock photo database Shutterstock in 2016. Although it was taken from a slightly different angle it shows many visual cues that overlap with the video, including the white triangular geometric patterns of the airport building roof, the dome to the left, the luggage transport vehicles and the open and closed doors of the plane. Other elements are missing. In the video, the light pole to the left of the aircraft appears without any lamps attached. The video is grainy and contains some visual glitches where parts of the image suddenly become blurry. When the supposed missile strikes the plane, a nearby vehicle significantly changes its shape as it is thrown into the air. Another inconsistency is that, despite the missile's massive explosion and a resulting fireball, nearby objects do not cast corresponding shadows. The account that shared the video has repeatedly posted AI-generated content in the past. Whereas the October 8 attack at King Khalid International Airport did reportedly badly damage a plane , this video does not show the moment of attack. Video predates attack and shows people move through objects Claim : This TikTok post with more than 301,000 views claims that the footage was recorded "just now from the heart of Riyadh Airport." AI-generated videos often contain impossible scenarios, like people walking through objects Image: Tik Tok DW Fact check : Fake This video had already circulated online in March 2026 , months before the attack. We found the video was shared in Greek , Albanian , Turkish and Russian . The footage contains several visual anomalies. Parts of the image appear blurry, and some people seem to merge into one another. In addition, a row of red lights in the terminal switches on one second before the supposed explosion becomes visible through the window. The clearest indication that the video is AI-generated is the way people move through the queue barriers. At the beginning of the video, several people appear to walk directly through them. After the supposed explosion, some individuals run straight through barriers that appear to end mid-air and are connected on only one side. Video contains Google AI watermarks Claim : This TikTok post , which has garnered more than 500,000 views, reports on the attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha and includes a compilation of videos. We examined the first video. Since August 2026, the EU's AI Act requires AI-generated content to carry machine-readable markings Image: Tik Tok DW Fact check : Fake Analysis using Google Gemini detected that the video was generated, at least in part, with Google AI tools. The clip contains a SynthID watermark in both the images and the audio. The same video also circulated on Facebook , where it has received more than 157,000 views. On Facebook it has been posted by an account that only shares AI-generated videos, and it is clearly labeled as "AI-content." All four videos examined by DW Fact check are very short. Two are between six and ten seconds long, while the other two last 13 and 15 seconds, respectively. Such brief videos are easier to create with AI and often contain very little visual information, making it difficult for viewers to verify their authenticity.
